title: It fits
hook: eyes fit light and seasons fit crops, he argues, as signs of providence (Discourses 1.6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: not more books, the athlete's shoulders, not his weights. Which reaction did you measure, and had it changed? Day three hundred ninety-five.

Hold up your hand and look at it. Your eye is doing something remarkable right now: catching light that bounced off your skin and turning it into a hand. But the eye alone would be useless in a dark room. Light alone, with no eye, would show nothing to anyone. They need each other. Neither one makes sense alone. Together, you see a hand. Epictetus noticed that, and built a whole chapter on it. Today: it fits.
screen: `LOOK AT YOUR HAND.` → `EYE WITHOUT LIGHT: USELESS.` → `THEY NEED EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Discourses book one, chapter six, is called on providence. Epictetus says a person needs two things to see it: the ability to take in everything that happens, and a grateful heart. Without gratitude, you'll see the same world and only complain. Then he builds his case from things that fit. Sight would be worth nothing if there were no colors and no light to see them by. Who made the one to match the other? And it isn't just the eye. There's the mind, which takes what the senses bring and sorts it, compares it, draws conclusions. That fits too. For the Stoics this fit is a sign that the world is ordered by reason, and that's what they mean by providence: not a God who fixes your parking tickets, but an intelligence woven through how things are made. People have argued about this for a long time. In Epictetus' own day, the Epicureans said the world came together by chance. Today some explain the fit between eye and light by evolution, some see design in it, and some see both. Epictetus' practical point doesn't wait for that argument to be settled. He ends the chapter by turning it inward: you, too, were fitted for something. You were given strength to bear what happens, patience, courage, a large spirit. So instead of crying that life is too hard, he says, notice what you were built to meet it with.
screen: `TWO THINGS: SEEING AND GRATITUDE.` · `EYE AND LIGHT FIT EACH OTHER.` · `THE STOIC MEANING OF PROVIDENCE.` · `YOU WERE FITTED TOO.` · then, large: `IT FITS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your eyes rest on something near you. Notice one fit. The breath and the air. Your hand and the cup it holds. The chair and the shape of you sitting in it. Stay with that one fit for a few breaths. Then turn inward and ask, gently: what have I been given that fits today's hard thing? Patience, humor, a friend, a little stubbornness. Name one. The bell holds the time.
It fits. Epictetus' way into providence: eye and light, mind and world, and our own strength matched to what we have to bear.
Your line: it fits. Today, notice one thing that fits something else so well you'd usually miss it, and let it make you a little grateful. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Some readers pair this chapter with a short gratitude practice: noticing one ordinary fit in the world, like eye and light, and one inner strength suited to the day's difficulty.

original.note: Greek pronoia: providence, literally 'forethought'; the title word of Discourses 1.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: providence means everything works out for me.
what it means: for the Stoics, the world's fit, eye with light and mind with world, shows a reason ordering it.
what a scholar hears: the argument from fit was a classic Stoic case against the Epicureans, who explained the world by atoms meeting by chance.
